title: The Seventh Day and the Garden in Eden
summary: God finishes his work, rests on the seventh day, and blesses and sanctifies it. The story then turns close up: the LORD God forms the man from the dust, breathes life into him, and places him in a garden in Eden to work it and keep it, with one tree forbidden. Finding no suitable partner among the animals, God builds a woman from the man's side, and the chapter closes with the first marriage and a couple naked and unashamed.
story: Genesis 1 showed the whole world from above. The first three verses here finish that account with a day unlike the others, a day with no work and no closing evening. Then, from verse 4, the camera comes down to ground level. The God who spoke galaxies into place now kneels in the dirt to shape a man, plants a garden, gives him work and a word to obey, and notices that something is not yet good. The chapter sets up everything the next one will break: the trees, the command, the man and the woman, their trust, and their unashamed openness to each other and to God. Readers who know how chapter 3 goes will feel the weight of verse 17 and verse 25.
historical:
Verse 4 introduces the first of the recurring headings that divide Genesis, This is the account of (in Hebrew, toledot, often translated generations). It also brings a new name for God: the LORD God. In most English Bibles LORD in small capitals stands for the personal name of Israel's God, written YHWH in Hebrew and probably pronounced something like Yahweh, which he later explains to Moses (Exodus 3). Chapter 1 used only the general word for God. Many critical scholars take this change, along with differences in style and order, as a sign that 2:4b to 3:24 comes from a different and possibly older source than chapter 1. Others read the two as deliberate companions: the first presents God as sovereign creator of everything, the second as the covenant LORD who is personally near to the people he has made.

The geography of verses 10 to 14 mixes the familiar and the unknown. The Hiddekel is the Tigris, and the Euphrates needs no explanation; both flow through Mesopotamia. The Pishon and the Gihon cannot be identified with confidence. Cush elsewhere in the Bible usually means the land south of Egypt (ancient Nubia, in modern Sudan), though some scholars suggest a region in Mesopotamia here, and Havilah is often placed in Arabia. Proposals for Eden's location range from the head of the Persian Gulf to the mountains of eastern Turkey. The text places Eden at the source of the world's great rivers without letting it be found on a map.
cultural:
Ancient kings planted gardens, enclosed parks full of trees and water that displayed their wealth and power, and temples were often built with gardens. Readers have long noticed that Eden is described in language that Israel later used for its sanctuary. God walks there (3:8), using a form of the verb later used for his presence among Israel's camp. Gold and onyx, the materials of the land beside the garden, reappear in the tabernacle and on the high priest's garments. The two verbs of verse 15, to cultivate (or serve) and to keep (or guard), are paired again for the Levites' care of the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8). And cherubim will guard Eden's eastern entrance (3:24) just as woven cherubim later mark the way into the holy place. On this reading Eden is the first sanctuary and the man its first priest as well as its gardener.

The making of the man also speaks into its world. Neighboring peoples told of humans formed from clay: in the Babylonian Atrahasis epic clay is mixed with the blood of a slain god, and Egyptian art shows the god Khnum shaping people on a potter's wheel. Genesis uses a potter's verb too, but the man is formed from humble dust and receives God's own breath. The pairing is the point: made of the same stuff as the ground, yet alive with a life that comes directly from God. The wordplay of Hebrew helps: the man is adam, taken from the adamah, the ground, and the woman is ishshah, taken from ish, man.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 3 close the seven-day account with its own threefold rhythm (the seventh day is named three times) and end without the familiar evening and morning. Verses 4 to 25 are a single narrative that moves from lack to fullness. It opens with a list of what is missing (no shrub, no plant, no rain, no man to work the ground) and closes with a man, a woman, a garden, and nothing hidden between them. Inside that frame the narrator builds suspense with a surprising sentence, “It is not good for the man to be alone” (verse 18), the first thing in Genesis called not good. The parade of animals delays the answer, and the chapter's climax is the man's first recorded words, a short poem of delight in verse 23. Verse 24 then steps outside the story to draw a lesson for every later reader, and verse 25 quietly sets the stage for chapter 3, where the word for naked is nearly the same as the word used for the serpent's craftiness.

outline.t: God rests on the seventh day and makes it holy
The LORD God forms the man and gives him breath
The garden in Eden and its four rivers
Work to do and a command to keep
Not good to be alone: the man names the animals
The woman, the first marriage, and no shame

doctrines.note: Human beings are dust and breath together: creatures made from the ground and dependent on it, yet given life by God's own breath. Work is part of the original good life in the garden, not a punishment that came later. The chapter also shows that humans were made for relationship; solitude is the first thing God calls not good.

Marriage appears here as God's gift, a man and a woman leaving their parents and being joined into one flesh. The woman is a partner who corresponds to the man, and the chapter ends with a union marked by trust and the absence of shame. Jesus returns to this passage as the pattern for marriage.

The first thing God sanctifies in the Bible is not a place or a person but a day. By resting and setting the seventh day apart, God builds rhythm and rest into the created order, the ground for Israel's later Sabbath.

Even in the garden, life with God includes a command. The prohibition in verses 16 and 17 is set inside overwhelming generosity (every other tree is freely given), and it frames obedience as trust in God's word about what is good.

words.note: Shavat, to cease or stop, often translated rested in verses 2 and 3. The word is not about recovering from tiredness but about stopping because the work is complete. The noun Sabbath comes from the same root, and Exodus 20:11 grounds Israel's weekly day of rest in this verse.

Nephesh, usually translated soul, but here in the phrase living being. The same phrase describes the animals in 1:20-24, so it does not mean a separate immortal part inside the body. It names the whole living, breathing creature. What sets the man apart in this verse is not the word nephesh but the personal breath of God that makes him one.

Ezer, helper. Modern ears can hear this as an assistant or subordinate, but in the Hebrew Bible the word is used most often of God himself as Israel's helper (for example Exodus 18:4 and Psalm 121:1-2). It describes help that supplies what is lacking. Paired with the phrase translated suitable (literally corresponding to him or opposite him), it presents the woman as the man's true counterpart.

Davaq, to cling or hold fast, translated be united in verse 24. It is used of a tongue sticking to the roof of the mouth and, in Deuteronomy, of Israel holding fast to the LORD. Here it describes the loyal, lasting bond of marriage, which is why the verse pairs it with leaving father and mother.

christ: Jesus quotes this chapter when he is asked about divorce. He joins Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 and concludes, “So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate” (Matthew 19:6), appealing to God's design from the beginning over later concessions. Paul quotes the same verse and adds, “This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32), so that marriage becomes a living picture of Christ's self-giving love for his people. Paul also takes up verse 7: “The first man Adam became a living being;” the last Adam a life-giving spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45), contrasting the one who received life with the risen Christ who gives it. The rest of the seventh day is picked up in Hebrews 4, which says “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), and the garden's river and tree of life return in Revelation 22 in the city where God dwells with his people. These are the New Testament's own readings, not codes hidden in Genesis 2.

hard.q: Does Genesis 2 contradict Genesis 1 on the order of creation?
hard.a:
Read side by side, the two chapters seem to differ. Genesis 1 has plants on day three, animals on day six, and humanity last, male and female together. Genesis 2 begins with no plants yet, forms the man, then plants a garden, then forms the animals, and finally makes the woman. Many critical scholars conclude that two older accounts with different orders have been placed side by side, and that the ancient editor did not see this as a problem because each account makes its own theological point.

Other readers argue that the chapters do not overlap in the way they seem to. Genesis 2:5 mentions shrubs and plants of the field, which may mean cultivated crops that need rain and human work, not all vegetation. The verb in 2:19 can be rendered had formed, as some translations do, describing animals already made rather than a new order of creation. On this view chapter 2 zooms in on the sixth day and arranges events by theme rather than strict sequence. Both groups agree that the final form of Genesis presents the chapters as complementary, the first giving the cosmic frame and the second the intimate story of the first human beings.

questions: The first thing God calls not good is the man being alone. What does that say about how you were made, and about the isolation many people live with?
Work appears in the garden before anything goes wrong. How might it change your view of your daily work to see it as part of the good life God designed?
God blesses a day of rest before there is any law commanding it. What would it take for you to receive rest as a gift rather than something to earn?
